summary.title: Annotations as Rollouts: Efficient and Scalable Reinforcement Learning for Video MLLMs

setting_and_object.category: Algorithm (RL post-training method for video multimodal LLMs)

details: On-policy RL post-training (e.g., GRPO) for video MLLMs is sample-inefficient: sampled groups contain few high-quality rollouts, and chain-of-thought generation makes rollout collection expensive.
Ground-truth annotations are used only to score rollouts, never as direct optimization targets.
OraRL: inject each ground-truth annotation into its on-policy group as an 'oracle rollout', i.e., a direct positive optimization target alongside sampled rollouts.
Naive injection causes 'advantage inversion': the high-reward oracle raises the group mean baseline and flips otherwise-positive policy advantages to negative.

Fix is a decoupled advantage estimator: the baseline is computed from policy rollouts only (oracle-free), while the oracle-policy reward gap modulates a directional gain on policy advantages and a separate detached oracle advantage term.
Sign-balanced pruning: keep only the oracle plus the strongest positive and strongest negative rollout per group, cutting rollout cost.
Video-ORA family of unified video-perception MLLMs spanning 0.8B to 9B parameters, trained on top of a backbone MLLM.
Models are trained to answer without chain-of-thought reasoning at inference.
RL post-training on large multi-task video prompt sets, scaled up to 100k prompts.
Cost measured as per-step time relative to supervised fine-tuning: OraRL 2.2x SFT, GRPO-with-CoT 4.9x SFT.
GRPO (with chain-of-thought rollouts) as the primary RL baseline; the untrained backbone MLLM as a scaling reference.
Prior best task-specific/generalist models per benchmark, plus proprietary models GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro on VSI-Bench.
Temporal grounding (mIoU), video object tracking (average overlap), video segmentation, and spatial-intelligence benchmarks (three-benchmark macro average, including VSI-Bench).
Inference latency measured as decoding time per response (CoT vs. no-CoT).

key_findings.finding: Annotations can serve as oracle rollouts inside the on-policy group, but only if the advantage estimator is decoupled to avoid advantage inversion.
key_findings.evidence: The paper identifies that a high-reward oracle inflates the group baseline and flips signs of otherwise positive policy advantages; OraRL's estimator computes the baseline from policy rollouts alone and uses the oracle-policy gap to scale a directional gain plus a detached oracle advantage term.

key_findings.finding: Sign-balanced pruning makes oracle-augmented RL substantially cheaper than CoT-based GRPO.
key_findings.evidence: Retaining only the oracle and the strongest rollout of each sign yields 2.2x SFT step time versus 4.9x for GRPO with chain-of-thought.

key_findings.finding: OraRL scales favorably with both model size and data volume.
key_findings.evidence: It surpasses its backbone across the 0.8B-9B range and outperforms GRPO as prompt count is scaled up to 100k.

key_findings.finding: The resulting Video-ORA-9B sets new bests across temporal, tracking, segmentation, and spatial-intelligence video tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Temporal mIoU 62.5 to 66.0, tracking AO 73.0 to 78.2, segmentation 64.3 to 70.4, three-benchmark spatial-intelligence macro average 51.0 to 56.1, and VSI-Bench 73.1 versus 55.0 (GPT-5) and 55.1 (Gemini-3-Pro).

key_findings.finding: Strong performance is obtained without chain-of-thought, giving large inference-latency savings.
key_findings.evidence: Video-ORA-9B decodes in 130 ms compared with 4,780 ms for CoT decoding.
